Explain your Jenkins pipeline architectu: Describe it as layered: a Jenkinsfile (declarative) checked into each repo defining stages (build, test, security scan, deploy), running on Jenkins agents (static or ephemeral Kubernetes pod agents for scalability), with a Shared Library providing common reusable steps across teams. Mention how promotion between environments is gated (manual approval for production) and how secrets/credentials are injected via the Credentials store rather than hardcoded.
What stages do you include in your CI/CD: A typical production pipeline: checkout, build/compile, unit test, static analysis/security scan (SAST, dependency scanning), containerize and push to a registry, deploy to a staging environment for integration tests, then a gated promotion (manual approval or automated canary analysis) to production with automated rollback on failure.
How do you integrate third-party tools l: Most integrate via a Jenkins plugin or a CLI/API call added as a pipeline stage - e.g. a Prisma Cloud image scan step that fails the build if critical vulnerabilities are found, or a Datadog step that sends deployment markers/events so dashboards show exactly when a deploy happened, correlating any post-deploy metric changes with the release. Credentials for these tools are stored in Jenkins Credentials and injected via `withCredentials`, never hardcoded in the Jenkinsfile.
What is a multi-stage Jenkins pipeline?: A pipeline organized into multiple sequential `stage` blocks (e.g. Build, Test, Deploy) within one `pipeline { stages { ... } }` definition, each shown as a distinct step in the Jenkins UI's stage view - this gives clear visibility into exactly which phase failed, and lets `when` conditions gate specific stages (e.g. only run Deploy on the main branch) without needing separate pipelines per branch type.
Your Jenkins pipeline suddenly starts fa: Check what changed right before the failures started - a dependency version that auto-updated, an expired credential/certificate, a Jenkins/plugin upgrade, or an external service (registry, cloud API) having an outage - since 'worked for hundreds of builds then suddenly broke' almost always points to an external change rather than the pipeline code itself. Compare the last successful build's console output/environment against the first failing one to pinpoint exactly what differs.
Where do you start troubleshooting\u2014: Start at the failure's exact error message and log output - it usually tells you which layer to go to next (a Jenkins step error means look at Jenkins/the pipeline; an application stack trace means look at the app; a cloud API error code means look at the cloud service). Avoid guessing which layer is at fault before reading the actual error - jumping straight to the wrong layer wastes the most time in live troubleshooting.
Design a complete CI/CD pipeline for a J: On merge to main: trigger build (Maven/Gradle compile), run unit tests and static analysis (SonarQube), build a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, push to Artifact Registry, deploy to a staging namespace and run integration tests, then promote to production via a canary rollout (Argo Rollouts or a weighted traffic split) with automated analysis against error rate/latency, rolling back automatically if the canary regresses, and full promotion plus a Slack/PagerDuty deployment notification once healthy.
Would you use a Scripted Pipeline or Dec: Declarative Pipeline by default - it has a clearer, more restricted structure (stages, steps, post-actions, built-in `when`/`options`) that's easier to read, lint, and maintain across a team, and covers the vast majority of real pipeline needs. Scripted Pipeline (full Groovy) is reserved for genuinely complex custom logic that declarative syntax can't express, often called from within a declarative pipeline via a `script {}` block rather than abandoning declarative structure entirely.
Which type of pipeline is called a Jenki: A Jenkinsfile is simply the file (checked into source control, typically named `Jenkinsfile`) containing either a Declarative or Scripted pipeline definition - 'Jenkinsfile' refers to the file/practice of pipeline-as-code, not a third pipeline type distinct from declarative/scripted.
How would you rate yourself in GCP out o: Give an honest, specific number backed by evidence rather than a rounded-up guess - e.g. '7/10: strong on GKE, IAM, and networking day-to-day; less hands-on with BigQuery/data services' - a specific, calibrated self-rating with reasoning is far more credible than a flat high number that later doesn't hold up under technical follow-up questions.
What are the advantages of Compute Engin: Compute Engine adds cloud-native capabilities on top of a VM: live migration during host maintenance (no downtime for most maintenance events), per-second billing and sustained-use/committed-use discounts, instant resizing and snapshotting, custom machine types for precise CPU/memory sizing, and tight integration with GCP IAM, networking, and managed instance groups for autoscaling - none of which a traditional on-prem or unmanaged VM gets out of the box.
What machine families are available in C: General-purpose (E2, N2, N2D, N1) for balanced workloads, Compute-optimized (C2, C2D) for CPU-intensive workloads like gaming/HPC, Memory-optimized (M2, M3) for large in-memory databases, and Accelerator-optimized (A2, G2) for GPU workloads like ML training/inference - choosing the right family/size is a cost and performance decision made per workload rather than defaulting to one family everywhere.
A production VM becomes unreachable. How: Check the VM's status and recent activity in the console first (is it running, did it just restart/get rescheduled), then check the Serial Port console output for boot-level issues if SSH itself is failing, check firewall rules and the VM's network tags/routes for anything recently changed, and check monitoring for a resource exhaustion event (OOM, disk full) right before it went unreachable - the serial console is the key tool when SSH itself is the thing that's broken.
If an entire GCP region goes down, what: This depends on the DR tier required: for critical services, an active-active or warm-standby multi-region deployment with data replicated cross-region (Cloud SQL cross-region replicas, multi-region GCS buckets) and a global load balancer that fails over automatically via health checks; for less critical services, a documented, periodically-tested runbook to restore from cross-region backups into a standby region within an agreed RTO/RPO. The key point to make is that DR strategy should match the actual criticality/cost tradeoff of the service, not a single one-size-fits-all answer.
How would you improve security in GCP?: Enforce least-privilege IAM (custom/predefined roles, no broad Owner/Editor grants, regular access reviews via IAM Recommender), use Workload Identity instead of service account keys, put sensitive workloads behind VPC Service Controls, enable Security Command Center for continuous posture monitoring, encrypt data with CMEK where compliance requires it, and ensure Cloud Audit Logs are enabled and retained for every project as the baseline for detection and forensics.
A VM in VPC-A cannot communicate with a: Confirm whether the VPCs are peered or connected via VPN/Interconnect at all (VPC Peering is not transitive, and peering must be explicitly established both ways), then check firewall rules on both sides (egress on VPC-A's VM, ingress on VPC-B's VM, since GCP firewalls are stateful but still need explicit allow rules), and check route tables to confirm each VPC has a route to the other's CIDR range. Use `gcloud compute firewall-rules list` and the VPC Network's 'Connectivity Test' tool to pinpoint exactly where the packet path breaks.
CPU utilization is only 20%, but applica: Low CPU with high latency points away from compute and toward I/O/waiting - check for a slow downstream dependency (database query latency, an external API call), network saturation or DNS resolution delays, thread pool/connection pool exhaustion (the app is waiting on a limited pool rather than actually working), or disk I/O wait if the app does heavy disk access. Distributed tracing, if available, is the fastest way to see exactly where time is being spent within a request rather than guessing at the layer.
Compare Cloud Run, GKE, Compute Engine,: Cloud Run is fully managed, serverless container hosting with scale-to-zero - best for stateless request-driven services with minimal ops overhead. GKE gives full Kubernetes control for complex, stateful, or highly customized workloads needing fine-grained orchestration. Compute Engine is raw VMs for workloads needing full OS-level control or that don't containerize well. App Engine (Standard) is a fully managed PaaS with automatic scaling for supported language runtimes, trading flexibility for even less operational overhead than Cloud Run.
What are the Kubernetes Service types?: ClusterIP (default, internal-only virtual IP), NodePort (exposes a static port on every node's IP, mainly used as a building block for external access), LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud load balancer for external access, the standard for production external-facing services), and ExternalName (maps a Service to an external DNS name via a CNAME, for referencing resources outside the cluster by an in-cluster service name).
A Service is not routing traffic to the: Check the Service's selector against the target Pods' labels first (`kubectl get endpoints <service>` - if it's empty, the selector doesn't match any Pod, which is the most common cause), then confirm the Pods are actually Ready (a Service only routes to Ready Pods), and check the targetPort matches the container's actual listening port. A mismatched label selector or a failing readiness probe accounts for the large majority of these cases.
The control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) makes global decisions and stores cluster state, typically managed for you on GKE. Worker nodes run the kubelet (manages Pod lifecycle on that node, talks to the API server), kube-proxy (implements Service networking rules), and a container runtime (containerd). Users and controllers interact exclusively through the API server, which is the single source of truth all other components read from and write to.
Which components communicate with each o: kubectl/clients talk to the API server; the scheduler watches the API server for unscheduled Pods and assigns them to nodes; the controller manager watches for desired-vs-actual state mismatches and reconciles them; kubelet on each node polls the API server for Pods assigned to it and reports status back; etcd is only ever talked to by the API server (nothing else accesses it directly) - this hub-and-spoke design through the API server is what keeps the system consistent and secure.
Where do ConfigMaps and Secrets fit into: They're stored as objects in etcd (via the API server) just like any other Kubernetes resource, and are consumed by Pods at creation time - either injected as environment variables or mounted as files into the container's filesystem. They decouple configuration/sensitive values from the container image, so the same image can run with different config across environments without rebuilding.
What deployment strategies are available: Rolling update (default for Deployments - gradually replaces old Pods with new ones, some of each running during the transition), Recreate (kills all old Pods before creating new ones - simple but causes downtime), and, via additional tooling like Argo Rollouts, Blue-Green (full new environment stood up, traffic switched all at once) and Canary (a small percentage of traffic shifted to the new version first, with automated analysis before full rollout).
Which deployment strategy do you prefer: Canary, when the tooling supports it (Argo Rollouts, a service mesh, or a managed platform's native canary support) - it limits blast radius by exposing the new version to a small fraction of real traffic first, with automated metric analysis deciding whether to proceed or auto-rollback, catching regressions before they affect all users. Rolling update is a reasonable default for lower-risk services where the operational overhead of canary tooling isn't justified.
HPA automatically adjusts the number of Pod replicas for a Deployment/StatefulSet based on observed metrics (CPU/memory via metrics-server by default, or custom/external metrics like request rate via Prometheus Adapter), scaling out under load and back in when load drops, within a configured min/max replica range. It requires resource requests to be set on the Pods, since scaling decisions are based on utilization relative to requests.
VPA observes a workload's actual CPU/memory usage over time and recommends (or in Auto mode, automatically applies via Pod restart) right-sized resource requests/limits, addressing over- or under-provisioned Pods rather than scaling replica count. It shouldn't control the same metric as HPA simultaneously (e.g. both scaling on CPU), since they can fight each other - a common pattern uses VPA for memory right-sizing and HPA for CPU or request-based horizontal scaling.
Pods are getting killed automatically. H: `kubectl describe pod` shows the last termination reason directly - `OOMKilled` (exit code 137, container exceeded its memory limit) is explicit and unambiguous. Node-level resource pressure shows up differently: check `kubectl describe node` for Pressure conditions (MemoryPressure, DiskPressure) and look for evictions in `kubectl get events`, which indicate the kubelet proactively evicted lower-priority Pods to protect the node itself, distinct from a single container being OOMKilled for exceeding its own limit.
Multiple pods are in CrashLoopBackOff. H: First priority is restoring service, not full root-causing: roll back to the last known-good image/version immediately (`kubectl rollout undo` or redeploying the prior tag) rather than debugging the crash live in production. Once traffic is stable, `kubectl logs --previous` and `describe pod` on the failed version identify the actual cause (bad config, missing dependency, OOM) for a proper fix before attempting to redeploy the new version again.
`FROM` (base image), `WORKDIR` (working directory), `COPY`/`ADD` (bring files into the image), `RUN` (execute build-time commands), `ENV` (set environment variables), `EXPOSE` (document listening port), `USER` (run as non-root), `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` (container startup command), and `ARG` (build-time-only variables).
How do you scan Docker images for vulner: Integrate a scanner (Trivy, Grype, Prisma Cloud, or Artifact Registry's built-in vulnerability scanning) as a CI/CD stage that runs on every image build and fails the pipeline if critical/high-severity vulnerabilities are found, rather than scanning ad hoc or only in production. Also scan base images periodically even without a code change, since new CVEs are discovered in existing base image layers over time.
What is a multi-stage Docker build?: A Dockerfile with multiple `FROM` statements, where an early stage with the full build toolchain produces artifacts that a later, minimal final stage copies in via `COPY --from=<stage>` - this keeps the production image small and free of build tools, source code, and secrets only needed during the build, reducing both image size and attack surface.
Do Docker containers have separate kerne: Containers share the host's Linux kernel - they are not full virtual machines with their own kernel. Isolation comes from kernel features (namespaces for process/network/filesystem isolation, cgroups for resource limits) rather than hardware-level virtualization, which is why containers are much lighter weight and faster to start than VMs, but also why a container can never run a different kernel or OS type than the host.
How does a container communicate with th: A container's processes make standard Linux system calls directly to the host kernel, just like any other process on the host - the container runtime (containerd/runc) sets up namespaces and cgroups at container creation time to scope what the process can see and how many resources it can use, but after that setup, syscalls go straight to the shared host kernel with no additional translation layer.
Design a multi-cloud deployment using Te: Use separate provider blocks/configurations per cloud (`provider "google"`, `provider "aws"`) within a structure of cloud-specific modules exposing a consistent interface (inputs/outputs) so higher-level configuration doesn't need to know provider-specific details, and keep state separated per cloud/environment rather than one shared state file. Abstract only what's genuinely common (naming conventions, tagging) - forcing every cloud-specific resource through an artificial common abstraction usually creates more complexity than it saves.
What are the basic Terraform commands?: `terraform init` (initialize providers/backend), `terraform plan` (preview changes), `terraform apply` (apply changes), `terraform destroy` (tear down managed resources), `terraform validate` (syntax/config check), `terraform fmt` (format code), and `terraform state` (subcommands for inspecting/modifying state directly).
What happens if the S3 bucket storing th: Terraform loses its record of what it manages, but the actual cloud resources still exist - the fix is recreating the state (via `terraform import` for each resource, tedious but mechanical) rather than the infrastructure itself being gone. This is exactly why the state bucket needs versioning enabled (S3 versioning or GCS object versioning) and deletion protection/MFA-delete, so an accidental delete is recoverable from a previous version rather than requiring a full manual re-import.
If the Terraform state becomes very larg: Split state by blast radius - separate state files per environment, per major component, or per team - rather than one monolithic state for the entire infrastructure, since a large state slows down every plan/apply and increases the blast radius of any lock contention or corruption. Use `terraform_remote_state` data sources or Terragrunt to reference outputs across the now-separated states where cross-references are still needed.
Did you create Terraform modules from sc: Answer honestly with specifics - which modules you authored versus consumed from the public registry, and one concrete example (what the module provisions, what inputs/outputs it exposes, why it was built as a module rather than inline resources) to demonstrate real module-design experience rather than just using `terraform-google-modules` off the shelf.
How many Terraform services/resources ha: Give a realistic, specific answer naming the actual resource types (e.g. GKE clusters, VPCs/subnets, Cloud SQL instances, IAM bindings, Cloud Storage buckets) rather than an inflated count - depth on the resources you actually name is what the follow-up questions will test, not the total number.
Where do you prefer to store Terraform s: A remote backend with native locking - GCS bucket with versioning enabled for GCP-centric work, or Terraform Cloud/Enterprise for built-in state management, run history, and policy-as-code - never local state for anything beyond a personal sandbox, since local state can't be safely shared or locked across a team.
How would you design a monitoring soluti: Layer the three observability pillars: metrics (per-service RED metrics - rate, errors, duration - collected via Prometheus/Cloud Monitoring), distributed tracing (to follow a request across service boundaries and pinpoint where latency accumulates), and centralized structured logging (correlated by a trace/request ID). Define SLOs per critical service and alert on SLO burn rate rather than raw metric thresholds, so alerts reflect actual user impact.
What is the difference between monitorin: Monitoring answers known questions you thought to ask in advance (is CPU high, is the error rate above X%) via pre-defined dashboards and alerts. Observability is the broader property of being able to ask new, previously unanticipated questions about system behavior from the data you're already collecting (metrics, logs, traces) - it's what lets you debug a novel failure mode you never built a specific dashboard for.
Have you used Prometheus and Grafana?: Answer with actual scope - whether you deployed/operated the Prometheus server and Alertmanager yourself (scrape config, retention, federation) or primarily consumed dashboards someone else set up, and whether you've written PromQL queries and alerting rules yourself versus just viewing existing Grafana dashboards.
How do you deploy Prometheus and Grafana: Most commonly via the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart on Kubernetes, which bundles Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, and sensible default dashboards/scrape configs for cluster and workload metrics in one deployment. For production, configure persistent storage for Prometheus's TSDB, set retention appropriate to storage budget, and consider Thanos/Cortex for long-term retention and multi-cluster federation if needed beyond a single Prometheus instance's scale.
How do you expose application metrics to: Instrument the application with a Prometheus client library exposing a `/metrics` HTTP endpoint in Prometheus text format, then configure Prometheus to scrape it - on Kubernetes, this is usually automated via a `ServiceMonitor` (Prometheus Operator) that tells Prometheus which Services to scrape based on label selectors, rather than manually editing scrape_configs for every new service.
How do you configure alerts?: Define alerting rules in Prometheus (PromQL expressions with a `for` duration to avoid firing on transient blips) that route to Alertmanager, which groups related alerts, deduplicates, and routes them to the right channel (Slack, PagerDuty) based on labels/severity, with silencing and inhibition rules to reduce noise during known maintenance windows or when a higher-severity alert already covers a lower-severity symptom.
Why do we use sudo instead of logging in: sudo provides an audit trail (every privileged command is logged with the actual user who ran it, not just 'root'), lets you grant fine-grained, revocable privileged access per user/command via /etc/sudoers instead of all-or-nothing root access, and avoids the risk of someone being permanently logged in as root where any mistake (or compromised session) has unrestricted system-wide impact.
Each file has three permission sets - owner, group, and others - each with read (r/4), write (w/2), and execute (x/1) bits, commonly shown as a 10-character string (e.g. `-rwxr-xr--`) or numeric mode (e.g. 754). Read lets you view a file's contents (or list a directory), write lets you modify it (or add/remove entries in a directory), and execute lets you run it as a program (or traverse into a directory).
Why should we avoid 777 permissions?: 777 grants read, write, and execute to everyone on the system (owner, group, and all other users), meaning any user or any process running as any user can read, modify, or execute that file - for anything containing sensitive data, configuration, or executable code, this removes any meaningful access control and is a common vector for privilege escalation or data tampering if any other account on the system is compromised.
Why do we have both /etc/passwd and /etc: /etc/passwd holds user account metadata (username, UID, GID, home directory, shell) and is world-readable since many system tools need to look up this information. /etc/shadow holds the actual password hashes and is readable only by root, separating sensitive credential data from the general-purpose, widely-readable account metadata - this split exists specifically so a password hash isn't exposed to every user on the system just because they need to read basic account info.
Write a shell script to find files with: `find / -type f -perm 777 2>/dev/null` - `-type f` restricts to regular files (not directories/symlinks), `-perm 777` matches the exact mode, and redirecting stderr to /dev/null suppresses permission-denied noise from directories the scanning user can't traverse. For a broader match including setuid/setgid variants, `-perm -777` (with a leading dash) matches any file with at least those bits set rather than requiring an exact mode.
How have you used Python in DevOps?: Concrete categories to draw on: automation scripts (cloud resource cleanup, config validation, log parsing), Infrastructure tooling (custom Kubernetes client-based tools, CI/CD helper scripts), and small internal services (a Flask/FastAPI wrapper around an internal API or a Slack bot for on-call tooling) - naming actual scripts/tools you've built is far more convincing than a general 'I use Python for scripting' claim.
Write a Python script to upload a file t:
import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

def upload_file(local_path, bucket_name, object_key):
    s3_client = boto3.client('s3')
    try:
        s3_client.upload_file(local_path, bucket_name, object_key)
        return True
    except ClientError as e:
        print(f'Upload failed: {e}')
        return False
boto3's upload_file handles multipart upload automatically for large files, and catching ClientError specifically (rather than a bare except) surfaces AWS-specific errors like missing permissions or a non-existent bucket clearly, rather than swallowing them silently.
`git status`, `git add`/`commit`, `git push`/`pull`, `git branch`/`checkout` (or `switch`), `git merge`/`rebase`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git stash`, and `git cherry-pick` - being ready to explain when you'd use each (especially the less obvious ones like stash and cherry-pick) matters more than just naming them.
How do you clone only a single branch fr: `git clone --single-branch --branch <branch-name> <repo-url>` clones only the history of that one branch instead of every branch, useful for CI jobs or large repos where you only need one branch and want to minimize clone time/size. Add `--depth 1` on top for a shallow clone (only the latest commit) when full history isn't needed either.
What is git cherry-pick?: `git cherry-pick <commit-hash>` applies the changes from a specific commit on another branch onto your current branch as a new commit, without merging the entire branch - useful for pulling a single bugfix from one branch into another (e.g. a hotfix that needs to land on both main and a release branch) without bringing in unrelated commits.
What is the difference between git clone: `git clone` creates a full local copy of a remote repository for the first time. `git fetch` downloads new commits/branches from the remote into your local repo's remote-tracking branches without touching your working branch. `git pull` is `git fetch` immediately followed by a merge (or rebase, with `--rebase`) into your current branch - `fetch` lets you inspect incoming changes before integrating them, while `pull` integrates immediately.
Have you worked with Argo CD?: Answer with actual scope - whether you set up and configured ArgoCD itself (Applications, Projects, RBAC, ApplicationSets) or primarily worked within an ArgoCD-managed environment someone else set up (making Git changes that ArgoCD then deployed). Both are legitimate experience, but the distinction matters for how deep to go on ArgoCD-specific configuration questions.
What is GitOps?: GitOps is an operating model where Git is the single source of truth for both application and infrastructure desired state, and a controller (ArgoCD, Flux) continuously reconciles the live environment to match what's declared in Git - deployments happen via Git commits/merges rather than someone running `kubectl apply` or a deploy script directly, giving a full audit trail, easy rollback (git revert), and automatic drift detection/correction.
What is your hands-on experience with Ar: Be specific: Applications/Projects you've configured, whether you've used App of Apps or ApplicationSets for scale, how you've handled secrets in the GitOps repo (Sealed Secrets/External Secrets Operator), and any incident you've debugged (an OutOfSync Application, a sync failure) - concrete specifics here demonstrate real operational experience versus just knowing ArgoCD's concepts.
How do you handle a production incident?: Assess and communicate impact first, mitigate quickly (rollback, scale, traffic shift) before fully root-causing if impact is significant, follow the team's incident process (declare severity, assign an incident commander for major incidents, keep a running timeline), and only move to full root cause analysis and a written postmortem once the immediate fire is out.
Do you log in directly to production ser: The mature answer is following process - using approved tooling (kubectl with RBAC, a bastion/jump host with audit logging, or an incident-management platform) rather than ad hoc direct logins, since direct unaudited access to production is both a security risk and makes post-incident review harder. Acknowledge that direct access is sometimes genuinely necessary for deep debugging, but even then it should go through an audited, time-boxed access mechanism, not standing credentials.
How do you communicate during a Sev-1 in: Establish a single incident channel/bridge immediately, post regular status updates on a fixed cadence (even 'still investigating, no update' is better than silence) so stakeholders aren't left guessing, designate one person as incident commander to avoid conflicting parallel efforts, and keep customer-facing communication (status page) synced with internal findings but appropriately abstracted for an external audience.
How do you improve application security: Layer defenses: input validation and output encoding to prevent injection attacks, dependency scanning to catch known-vulnerable libraries, secrets management (never in code/config files), least-privilege service accounts/IAM for the app's own permissions, network segmentation (the app shouldn't be able to reach services it doesn't need), and regular penetration testing/security review rather than a one-time security pass at launch.
How do you manage secrets securely?: Use a dedicated secrets manager (Secret Manager, Vault) as the source of truth, never commit secrets to source control or bake them into container images, inject them at runtime (via Workload Identity + Secret Manager API calls, or an operator like External Secrets syncing into Kubernetes Secrets), rotate them regularly, and scope access via IAM so only the specific services that need a given secret can read it.
How do you secure Docker images?: Use minimal base images (distroless or alpine) to reduce attack surface, run as a non-root user, scan images for vulnerabilities in CI and block builds with critical findings, sign images and verify signatures at deploy time (Cockpit/cosign) to prevent tampering, and use multi-stage builds so build tools and secrets never end up in the final image.
Do you have any questions for us?: Always have 2-3 ready and specific to what was discussed - one on technical depth (their current architecture or biggest platform challenge), one on team/process (on-call structure, how incidents are reviewed), and one on growth (what success looks like in the first 90 days). Avoid questions answerable from the job posting, and skip compensation/PTO questions in a technical round.
What kind of role are you looking for?: Be specific and consistent with what you've emphasized throughout the interview - name the scope (IC vs. some leadership), the domain (platform/SRE/MLOps), and what draws you to this specific type of role, rather than a vague 'anything challenging' answer that gives the interviewer nothing to match you against.
Do you have any feedback for us?: If genuine, keep it constructive and specific (e.g. praising a well-structured interview process, or noting a question that felt ambiguous) rather than generic flattery or an unfiltered complaint - this is a low-stakes question but still visible, so keep it professional and brief.
Is there anything else you\u2019d like t: Use this as a final chance to ask about anything not yet covered that would genuinely affect your decision (team structure, tech stack details, growth path) rather than repeating an earlier question - or, if everything's been covered, a brief 'No, I think we've covered everything - thank you for the thorough conversation' closes the interview professionally.

Debug and improve the following shell sc:
Issues: the smart/curly quotes (“”) around the path are not valid shell string delimiters (must be straight double quotes), and while `Search_path` (mixed case) works in bash, lowercase or snake_case is the shell scripting convention to avoid colliding with environment/built-in variable naming patterns. Scanning from `/` unscoped will also traverse mounted network filesystems, /proc, and other pseudo-filesystems, producing noise and potentially hanging on slow mounts. Improved version:

#!/bin/bash
search_path="/"
find "$search_path" -xdev -type f -perm 0777 2>/dev/null
`-xdev` keeps the search within one filesystem (won't descend into other mounted filesystems), and `0777` is the more explicit/conventional way to write the exact permission mode, though `777` and `0777` are functionally equivalent to find.
